subject: chemistry_2
question_text: Describe the two main types of semiconductors and contrast their conduction mechanism.

verification.note: Unit 1 (Solid State) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", book p.63, which prints the question and a model answer. The 1+1+1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK STRUCTURE: the printed answer answers "two main types" as intrinsic and extrinsic first, and only then reaches n-type and p-type. The question asks for a contrast of CONDUCTION MECHANISM, and only the n-type and p-type pair differ in mechanism, so this card treats those as the two main types and keeps intrinsic and extrinsic as a one line lead-in. BOOK ERROR: the printed answer lists nitrogen among the n-type dopants, "VA group elements (N, P, As)". Nitrogen is in group 15 but is not used to dope silicon or germanium; NCERT names phosphorus and arsenic. This card writes P, As and Sb. Indium is listed with the group 13 dopants here because the book's own next question dopes germanium with indium.

steps.label: Semiconductors and doping
lines: A semiconductor is a solid whose electrical
conductance lies between that of a conductor
and that of an insulator.
Pure silicon and germanium are intrinsic
semiconductors, and their conductivity is too
low to be of practical use.
Adding a small measured amount of a
suitable impurity raises the conductivity.
This process is called doping, and the
product is an extrinsic semiconductor.
steps.why: Doping is the step that creates both of the types the question asks about, so it has to come first. A pure crystal has every valence electron locked in a bond; the impurity is what supplies either a spare electron or a missing one.
common_mistakes: Writing that doping adds a large amount of impurity. Only a very small measured amount is added.
Calling pure silicon an extrinsic semiconductor. Pure silicon is intrinsic; doping it makes it extrinsic.
steps.memory_tip: Intrinsic means pure, extrinsic means doped. Doping is the only difference between them.
steps.margin_note: Define semiconductor and doping in the first three lines. Both terms are used in every later step.

steps.label: n-type
lines: n-type: silicon or germanium is doped with a
group 15 element such as P, As or Sb.
The dopant atom has 5 valence electrons.
Four of them form bonds with the four
neighbouring silicon atoms and the fifth is
left over.
This extra electron is free to move, so the
current is carried by negative electrons.
steps.why: Silicon forms four bonds, so a dopant with five valence electrons has one electron more than the bonding needs. That electron is not held in any bond, so a small applied voltage moves it and the crystal conducts.
common_mistakes: Writing that the crystal now has a negative charge. The dopant atom is itself neutral, so the crystal stays neutral; only the way it conducts changes.
Doping with a group 13 element and calling it n-type. Group 15 gives n-type, group 13 gives p-type.
steps.memory_tip: n is for negative. Five valence electrons, one spare, and the spare is negative.
steps.margin_note: The number 5 and the phrase "extra electron" are the two scoring items. Name at least one dopant element.

steps.label: p-type
lines: p-type: silicon or germanium is doped with a
group 13 element such as B, Al, Ga or In.
The dopant atom has only 3 valence
electrons, so one of the four bonds is short
of an electron.
That empty place in the bond is called a hole
and has the effect of a positive charge.
An electron from a neighbouring bond moves
into the hole, and the hole moves the other
way, so the current is carried by holes.
steps.why: A dopant with three valence electrons cannot complete the fourth bond, and the empty place left behind is the hole. Electrons hop into it one after another, which is the same as the hole travelling in the opposite direction, and a moving hole carries current just as a moving electron does.
common_mistakes: Writing that a hole is a proton or a positive ion. A hole is an empty place in a bond, nothing more.
Saying the crystal is positively charged. The crystal stays neutral; the hole only has the effect of a positive charge.
steps.memory_tip: p is for positive. Three valence electrons, one bond short, and the gap acts positive.
steps.margin_note: The number 3 and the word "hole" are the two scoring items. Say that the hole moves opposite to the electrons.

steps.label: The contrast
lines: n-type: group 15 dopant, one extra electron,
negative carrier.
p-type: group 13 dopant, one missing
electron, positive carrier.
In both, the crystal as a whole stays neutral.
steps.why: The question asks for a contrast, so the two mechanisms have to be set side by side in one place. The dopant group determines everything else: group 15 leaves a spare electron and group 13 leaves a hole, and the carrier follows from that.
common_mistakes: Describing the two types but never comparing them. The word contrast means the comparison itself is being marked.
Swapping the groups. Group 15 gives n-type and group 13 gives p-type.
steps.memory_tip: Group 15 is one above four bonds, so a spare electron. Group 13 is one below, so a hole.
steps.margin_note: Two boxed lines side by side are enough for this mark. Add the dopant group to each line.

insider_note: The word contrast is the instruction that carries the last mark, so finish with the two mechanisms written side by side. Do not name nitrogen as a dopant; write phosphorus or arsenic.
